notes: Deposit forfeiture clause construction on summary judgment appeal; Lightman J's reasoning is clear and complete.

enrichment.short_title: Ashfield Land v Mallan: deposit forfeiture under conditional property contract
key_facts: Ashfield Land paid a £600,000 deposit under a £6 million contract to buy Park Court, Coventry, conditional on entering a Council Contract for adjacent council land.
Cabinet approval of Heads of Terms was given on 18 February 2003, but by 28 May 2003 no final Council Contract document existed despite five drafts exchanged with Coventry CC.

Mallan rescinded under clause 11.3 and claimed forfeiture of the deposit under clause 11.5, arguing Coventry CC was ready, willing and able to exchange terms in substantial accordance with the Heads of Terms.
Master Bragge granted summary judgment for repayment; Lightman J heard the appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from summary judgment under CPR Part 24 on whether the vendor had a real prospect of forfeiting the deposit.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Master Bragge's summary judgment for repayment of the £600,000 deposit upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Clause 11.5 required an existing final-form Council Contract in substantial accordance with the Heads of Terms which Coventry CC was ready to exchange; readiness to contract in substance without a proffered document, or advanced negotiations short of a final document, does not trigger forfeiture.
legal_issues: Whether clause 11.5 required an agreed final contract document on the critical date or only substantive readiness to exchange
Whether condition 1(b) on reasonable cooperation by the purchaser applied
Whether summary judgment was appropriate on the pleaded facts

confidence.notes: Single issue of construction with clear factual background and explicit dispositive reasoning.

notes: Brussels II jurisdiction point on divorce pleading; Court of Appeal reasoning is concise and authoritative.

enrichment.short_title: Rogers-Headicar: Brussels II jurisdiction and divorce petition pleading
key_facts: The parties married in 2001, moved to Germany in 2002, and the wife returned to London in March 2003 and issued a divorce petition pleading habitual residence grounds.
Following Hague Convention child-return proceedings before Munby J, the husband challenged jurisdiction and later issued his own German-centred petition.
Wilson J allowed the wife to amend her pleaded jurisdictional basis to habitual residence of the applicant, condemning her in costs thrown away.
The husband appealed, contending jurisdiction depended on the pleaded grounds in the petition and that amendment impermissibly preserved priority of the English court.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission granted on whether a Brussels II jurisdictional amendment was permissible and on costs.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted but appeal dismissed; the court must determine jurisdiction under Article 2 independently of the form of pleading.
enrichment.ratio: Under Brussels II the court has an independent duty to determine whether jurisdiction exists under Article 2; Family Proceedings Rules require jurisdictional grounds to be stated in the petition for administrative efficiency but pleading does not confer or deny jurisdiction, and spurious petitions are exposed at preliminary issue with costs consequences.
legal_issues: Whether Brussels II jurisdiction is constrained by the grounds pleaded in the divorce petition
Whether Wilson J permissibly allowed late amendment of jurisdictional basis
Whether the costs award was unduly limited

confidence.notes: Short focused appellate ruling on a settled Brussels II principle with clear order.

notes: Attorney General reference on lenient cannabis sentences; outcome and agreed basis of plea are clearly recorded.

enrichment.short_title: AG Reference: lenient sentences for 120kg cannabis transport
key_facts: Hiscock and Coombes pleaded guilty to possession of cannabis with intent to supply after 120 kilograms in 240 packages were found in a Mercedes van, with estimated street value exceeding £500,000.
An agreed basis of plea stated they were paid £400 each for a one-off transport on 19 July 2003 without prior contact with the drugs or ongoing involvement.
Each received two years' imprisonment at Woolwich Crown Court despite good character and ample evidence of conspiracy to supply.
The Attorney General referred the sentences as unduly lenient.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988.
enrichment.outcome: Leave granted but reference dismissed; sentences were lenient but not increased having regard to the agreed basis of plea and double jeopardy.
enrichment.ratio: Sentencing must reflect an agreed basis of plea even where it appears unrealistic; where the court allows for double jeopardy on a lenient sentence tied to a limited-role basis accepted by the Crown, increase may be inappropriate despite concern about the basis itself.
legal_issues: Whether two-year sentences were unduly lenient for 120kg cannabis
Whether the agreed limited-role basis of plea should have been accepted
Application of Aramah and Lee Odey sentencing guidance
Effect of double jeopardy on an Attorney General reference
linked_authorities: R v Aramah (1982)
R v Lee Odey [2001] 2 Cr App R(S) 85

confidence.notes: Facts, basis of plea and measured dismissal are explicit though the court expressed concern about the plea agreement.

notes: Reserved libel judgment on absolute privilege at child protection conferences; lengthy but dispositive on the privilege issue.

enrichment.short_title: W v Westminster: absolute privilege and child protection conference report
key_facts: A 70-year-old stepfather of a child challenged words in a March 2003 child protection review report suggesting he might be grooming his stepdaughter for prostitution.
Publication to five conference attendees was admitted; the council later conceded the grooming reference should not have been included.
Westminster City Council pleaded absolute privilege for the social workers' report prepared for a Child Protection Case Conference under the Children Act 1989.
Tugendhat J heard the absolute privilege issue by judge alone after allowing a late amendment and ordering trial without jury.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Reserved interlocutory judgment at trial on whether words in a child protection conference report were published on an occasion of absolute privilege.
enrichment.outcome: Absolute privilege rejected; the occasion was one of qualified privilege, with malice to be assessed in the exceptional Horrocks v Lowe sense applicable to relaying allegations without endorsing them.
enrichment.ratio: Communications at Child Protection Case Conferences are not occasions of absolute privilege; necessity for immunity is not shown where qualified privilege and case management can protect frank multi-agency reporting, and competing Article 8 rights of child and claimant require a case-by-case balance rather than blanket immunity.
legal_issues: Whether absolute privilege extends to local authority child protection conference reports
Effect of Waple and S v Newham and post-HRA developments
Whether D v East Berkshire supports absolute privilege in defamation
Appropriate malice test where social workers report allegations without endorsing truth
linked_authorities: Waple v Surrey County Council [1998] 1 WLR 860
S v Newham London Borough Council [1998] 1 FLR 1061
Horrocks v Lowe [1975] AC 135
X v Bedfordshire CC [1995] 2 AC 633

confidence.notes: Core privilege ruling is clear though trial issues on meaning, relevance and malice remained for later resolution.

notes: Renewed JR application on Crown Court adjournment refusal; permission granted and decision quashed by agreement.

enrichment.short_title: Reynolds v Ipswich Crown Court: judicial review of refused appeal adjournment
key_facts: Reynolds was convicted in October 2003 of harassment arising from a boundary dispute with neighbours Dr and Mrs Kelly after a protracted magistrates' court trial.
His Crown Court appeal was adjourned twice when he was in New Zealand with medical certificates stating he was unfit to fly.
On 10 May 2004 he was unrepresented, still abroad, and HHJ Holt refused a further adjournment, finding no proper intention to prosecute the appeal; the appeal was heard in his absence and dismissed.
Reynolds sought judicial review of the refusal to adjourn.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to apply for judicial review of the Crown Court's refusal to adjourn a section 2 harassment appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted; on agreement the 10 May decision was quashed and the matter remitted to Ipswich Crown Court with costs to the claimant.
enrichment.ratio: It is arguable that a Crown Court erred in finding no proper intention to prosecute an appeal where medical evidence supported unavoidable absence, giving insufficient weight to prejudice from proceeding in the appellant's absence contrary to Rowlands and Booth principles.
legal_issues: Whether refusal to adjourn deprived the appellant of a fair opportunity to present his case
Whether the court wrongly inferred lack of intention to prosecute the appeal
Proper weight to be given to medical evidence of unfitness to travel
Balancing interests of appellant, witnesses and public in adjournment decisions
linked_authorities: R v Hereford Magistrates' Court ex p Rowlands [1998] QB 110
R v Birmingham City Magistrates' Court ex p Booth [1999] EWHC Admin 425
R v Chaaban [2003] EWCA Crim 1012

confidence.notes: Permission reasoning and agreed quashing order are clearly recorded though detailed substantive review was not required.

notes: Section 14A Limitation Act appeal on solicitor negligence; Arden LJ's analysis is detailed and definitive.

enrichment.short_title: Gravgaard v solicitors: section 14A limitation and negligent mortgage advice
key_facts: Mrs Gravgaard inherited a Bournemouth house in 1982 and in March 1988 was advised by solicitors to transfer it into joint names and mortgage to Wessex Building Society to support her husband's business.
She alleged the deed of gift was unnecessary because Wessex would have lent on her sole title with her husband as guarantor, exposing the home to her husband's creditors.
Further Lloyds guarantees and charges followed in 1988; possession proceedings and charging orders arose from 1993 onwards.
Proceedings against the solicitors were issued in May 2002; the recorder held the claim statute-barred under section 14A with constructive knowledge by end of 1996.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from county court dismissal on limitation after findings of solicitor negligence were made.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the claim was time-barred with constructive knowledge attributable from late 1988 or at latest December 1996.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 14A(10) a claimant may be expected to seek appropriate expert advice when serious property exposure arises; knowledge discoverable through investigating one claim (against a bank) can be imputed for a related negligence claim against a solicitor, and the subsection requires regard to the actual claimant's circumstances rather than a wholly hypothetical reasonable person.
legal_issues: When Mrs Gravgaard acquired the knowledge required under section 14A(5) and (6)
Whether investigating claims against Lloyds should have revealed a claim against the solicitors
Construction of 'appropriate expert advice' in section 14A(10)
Whether March 1988 and September 1988 transactions were inextricably linked for limitation purposes
index_terms: Royal Bank of Scotland v Etridge
linked_authorities: Royal Bank of Scotland v Etridge (No 2) [2002] 2 AC 773
Adams v Bracknell Forest BC [2004] 3 WLR 89
Hallam-Eames v Merrett Syndicates [2001] Lloyds Law Rep PN 178

confidence.notes: Detailed limitation analysis with clear factual chronology and affirmance of the recorder's conclusion.

notes: Sentence appeal under Sexual Offences Act 2003; reduction and Millberry guidance application are clear.

enrichment.short_title: R v Wisniewski: reduced sentences for battery with intent to commit sexual offence
key_facts: Wisniewski, a Polish national of previous good character, committed two night-time street attacks on lone women in Devon in June 2004.
The first incident involved grabbing a woman who escaped over a wall; the second involved dragging a woman into a churchyard intending rape before a neighbour intervened.
He pleaded guilty at the earliest opportunity to two counts of battery with intent to commit a sexual offence under section 62 and was sentenced to seven years total with deportation recommended.
The judge was held to have started too high and insufficiently reflected the guilty pleas and absence of Millberry aggravating features.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against sentence by leave of the Single Judge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; sentences reduced from two years plus five consecutive to 18 months plus three-and-a-half years (five years total); deportation order stood.
enrichment.ratio: Battery with intent under the 2003 Act should generally attract lower sentences than rape or attempted rape in similar circumstances given the ten-year maximum; pre-Act authorities including Millberry guide sentencing, but a judge must not treat all Millberry aggravating features as present and must give full credit for earliest guilty pleas.
legal_issues: Appropriate starting points for section 62 battery with intent
Application of R v Millberry aggravating features
Credit for earliest guilty pleas
Whether consecutive sentences totalling seven years were manifestly excessive
linked_authorities: R v Millberry [2003] 2 Cr App R(S) 142
Attorney-General's References Nos 91, 119 and 120 of 2002 [2003] 2 Cr App R(S) 338

notes: Major s288 planning challenge to Holford gas storage permission; lengthy judgment but clear dismissal on all grounds.

enrichment.short_title: Cranage Parish Council: challenge to Holford underground gas storage permission
key_facts: Scottish Power sought planning permission for solution mining, underground gas cavities, pipelines and processing plant on over 200 hectares at Holford Brinefield near Northwich, Cheshire.
Local planning authorities refused the application; after a public inquiry the inspector recommended refusal, but the Secretaries of State granted permission on 19 May 2004.

Cranage Parish Council and three individual residents challenged the decision under section 288, arguing misinterpretation of local plan policy PS1, failure to consider relevant matters, and Article 8 infringement.
The scheme involved major accident hazard concerns in a rural area above brine cavities linked to Ineos Chlor's salt extraction operations.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 statutory challenge to a recovered planning appeal decision of the Secretaries of State.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed on all grounds; permission to appeal refused; costs ordered against claimants subject to indemnity arrangements.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 18A and ex parte Woods, a decision-maker may reasonably interpret development plan policy PS1 as two related policies and depart from the plan where material considerations including energy need outweigh harm; Article 8 does not require alternative-site analysis in planning balance, and absence of the word 'proportionality' does not invalidate a fair balancing exercise compliant with Lough.
legal_issues: Whether VRBLP policy PS1 supported or precluded the gas storage development
Whether the Secretaries of State failed to consider relevant inspector findings and safety concerns
Whether Article 8 and proportionality required individualised assessment of affected residents
Lawfulness of departure from the development plan under section 18A
linked_authorities: R v Secretary of State for the Environment ex parte Wood [1995] JPL 731
Lough v First Secretary of State [2004] EWCA Civ 1077
Samaroo v Secretary of State [2001] EWCA Civ 555

confidence.notes: Very long judgment but dispositive conclusions on development plan, material considerations and human rights are explicit.

notes: Solicitors Act s70 special circumstances appeal; Beatson J's reasoning on misleading costs letter is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Kundrath v Kwatia: special circumstances for late bill taxation
key_facts: Sylvia Kundrath received a solicitors' bill for £23,746.05 from Henry Kwatia & Gooding in July 2002 for defending management company proceedings.
She disputed the bill in August 2002 and the firm replied that taxation required her to apply to court and that after one month an order would be conditional on paying 40% into court.
Master Rogers refused her March 2004 application for detailed assessment as outside twelve months without special circumstances.
The firm later pursued bankruptcy via statutory demand; Beatson J heard her appeal with permission.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a costs master's refusal to order detailed assessment of a solicitor's bill more than twelve months after delivery.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; special circumstances found and detailed assessment ordered, with bankruptcy proceedings to be stayed pending assessment.
enrichment.ratio: Special circumstances under section 70(3) are assessed in the aggregate; a solicitor's misleading letter inducing belief that taxation required a 40% payment into court can amount to improper pressure dissuading a lay client from seeking assessment, and unresolved uncertainty about retainer termination at billing may also constitute special circumstances.
legal_issues: Whether the client's delay beyond twelve months was excused by special circumstances
Whether the 19 August 2002 letter amounted to improper pressure
Whether retainer status and absence of a client care letter were relevant
Scope of appellate review of a costs judge's discretion
linked_authorities: Arrowfield Services Ltd v BP Collins [2003] EWHC 830 (Ch)
Re Norman (1886) 16 QBD 673
Sanders v Isaacs [1971] Ch 240

confidence.notes: Dispositive reasoning on special circumstances and fresh exercise of discretion is clearly expressed.

notes: Commercial Court preliminary issues on aircraft reinsurance cut-through and repair agreement; Langley J's findings are comprehensive.

enrichment.short_title: Grecoair v reinsurers: direct claim and March 1997 repair agreement
key_facts: Grecoair dry-leased a Boeing 707 cargo aircraft to Angola Air Charter; ENSA insured AAC with Grecoair as additional insured and London market reinsurers covered hull and liability risks with deductibles.
Grecoair claimed two accidents in 1994/95 caused substantial fuselage damage but notified reinsurers late and disputed whether damage was accident-related or due to corrosion and poor maintenance.
After disputed Boeing, GAMCO and FLS repair estimates, a meeting at the Butler Syndicate on 11 March 1997 led Grecoair to claim reinsurers agreed FLS would repair the aircraft.
Reinsurers contended Grecoair must claim through ENSA in Angola and that no binding repair agreement was made.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of preliminary issues ordered by Tomlinson J on direct reinsurance claims and alleged March 1997 repair agreement.
enrichment.outcome: Grecoair failed on both issues; no direct right to sue reinsurers and no binding agreement to repair; the claim is unsustainable on those bases.
enrichment.ratio: Reinsurance 'Information' clauses record underlying policy terms for ENSA's cover rather than conferring direct rights on an additional insured; statements at the March 1997 meeting about being 'happy to repair' accident damage were not a formal offer capable of acceptance where parties disputed what repairs were required and who bore responsibility for non-accident damage.
legal_issues: Whether Grecoair could sue reinsurers directly under reinsurance wording and certificates
Whether a binding agreement to repair via FLS was made on 11 March 1997
Construction of AVN 67A additional insured and hold-harmless provisions
Effect of AVN 41 claims control on settlement authority

confidence.notes: Preliminary issue findings are detailed and conclusive though quantum and policy defences were reserved if issues had failed for reinsurers.
